title: Risk assessment: two-tier health check framework
summary: The proposed two-tier health check framework (Approach A) is architecturally sound and well-aligned with existing codebase patterns. The primary risks center on (1) integration complexity with the 5543-line routes/pipelines.py, (2) concurrency hazards where health check state mutations race with signal handlers and the container monitor thread, (3) introducing an LLM dependency (Anthropic API) into the orchestrator for the first time, and (4) the scope of the change (~13 new files, modifications to 8 existing files across the critical path). No risks are blocking, but three require human review: the pipelines.py integration strategy, the decision on whether Tier 2 should ship in the same change or as a fast-follow, and the FAIL_PIPELINE auto-enforcement behavior.

approach_reviewed.name: Unified HealthCheck interface with HealthCheckRunner
approach_reviewed.verdict: Proceed with caution. The architecture is well-designed. Key risks are manageable with the mitigations outlined below.

risks.title: Integration with routes/pipelines.py (_run_pipeline) is high-touch and fragile
risks.description: routes/pipelines.py is 5543 lines and contains the central orchestration loop (_run_pipeline at line 3965). The architect's plan calls for wiring HealthCheckRunner.run_checks(trigger=PHASE_COMPLETE) into the phase transition logic and passing on_wave_complete callbacks. Currently, execute_all_waves() is called at line 3260 WITHOUT an on_wave_complete callback — adding one changes the calling pattern. The file handles review cycles, phase transitions, error recovery, and multi-agent coordination. A bug in health check wiring here could silently break pipeline execution or cause pipelines to be incorrectly marked FAILED.
evidence: routes/pipelines.py is 5543 lines — largest file in the orchestrator
execute_all_waves() at line 3260 is called without on_wave_complete today; adding a callback changes the execution pattern
_run_pipeline() at line 3965 is a complex state machine with multiple branching paths for phase transitions
Any exception thrown by a health check callback during wave/phase completion would propagate into the pipeline execution thread

steps: Wrap all HealthCheckRunner.run_checks() calls in try/except at the integration site — health check failures must NEVER propagate to the pipeline execution thread
Keep integration to exactly 2 call sites in pipelines.py: (1) pass on_wave_complete callback to execute_all_waves(), (2) call run_checks(PHASE_COMPLETE) after phase completion
The on_wave_complete callback should be a simple wrapper that catches all exceptions and logs them — it must not re-raise
Add integration tests that verify: (a) health check exception does not crash _run_pipeline, (b) health check timeout does not block phase transition
Do NOT restructure _run_pipeline() — changes should be purely additive (2-3 line insertions)

risks.rollback_plan: Revert the 2-3 lines that wire health checks into pipelines.py. The HealthCheckRunner and all checks can remain deployed but inactive — they are inert without trigger wiring.
risks.human_review_reason: The exact insertion points in _run_pipeline() should be reviewed by someone familiar with the phase transition control flow to ensure no edge cases are missed (e.g., short-circuit paths, error recovery branches).

risks.title: Concurrent state mutations from health checks and existing writers
risks.description: The HealthCheckRunner._apply_result() must mutate pipeline state when appending HealthCheckResult to PhaseExecution.health_checks and when applying FAIL_PIPELINE actions. This competes with concurrent writers: the container monitor reconciliation handler (background thread), signal handlers (HTTP thread), and _run_pipeline (pipeline thread). The existing per-pipeline RLock and optimistic versioning handle this correctly IF used consistently, but the HealthCheckRunner introduces a new writer that must follow the same patterns. A subtle bug (e.g., forgetting expected_version, holding the lock during LLM calls) could cause lost updates or deadlocks.
evidence: state_store.py uses per-pipeline RLock via get_pipeline_state_lock() and optimistic versioning via expected_version
container_monitor._reconcile_container_state() already uses this pattern but does NOT retry on VersionConflictError — it logs and returns False
The HealthCheckRunner will be called from multiple threads: pipeline execution thread (WAVE_COMPLETE, PHASE_COMPLETE), container monitor thread (RUNTIME_TICK), HTTP thread (ON_DEMAND)
Tier 2 checks take up to 30 seconds (LLM call) — if the lock is held during this time, all other writers for that pipeline are blocked

mitigation.strategy: Strict lock discipline and separation of evaluation from mutation
steps: HealthCheck.check() must be a PURE function: context in, result out. No locks held during check execution, especially during Tier 2 LLM calls
HealthCheckRunner.run_checks() should execute checks WITHOUT holding any lock, collect results, then acquire the per-pipeline lock ONLY for the brief _apply_result() step
_apply_result() must follow the exact same load-modify-save-with-expected_version pattern as _reconcile_container_state()
On VersionConflictError in _apply_result(), reload pipeline state and check if the pipeline is already FAILED (short-circuit) — do NOT blindly retry the mutation
Add a test that runs health checks and signal handlers concurrently on the same pipeline and verifies no VersionConflictError goes unhandled

risks.rollback_plan: If concurrency bugs emerge in production, disable health check state persistence (skip _apply_result() for result storage) while keeping event emission. Events are fire-and-forget via the async EventBus and have zero concurrency risk.

risks.title: Introducing Anthropic API dependency into the orchestrator (Tier 2)
risks.description: The orchestrator currently makes ZERO LLM API calls. All Claude interactions happen inside agent sandbox containers. The Tier 2 agent inspector introduces a direct Anthropic API dependency into the orchestrator process for the first time. This creates new failure modes: API key configuration, SDK dependency management, API rate limits, response parsing, and cost accumulation. The orchestrator is a long-running server process — an LLM client that leaks connections or handles errors poorly could degrade orchestrator stability over time.
evidence: grep for 'anthropic' in orchestrator/ returns zero matches for SDK imports (only 'claude' appears in prompt strings)
No anthropic SDK import exists anywhere in the orchestrator codebase
The architect's plan introduces orchestrator/health/llm_client.py as a new Anthropic SDK wrapper
The orchestrator runs as a single Flask server process with waitress (16 threads) — an unhandled LLM client error on one thread could affect others if state is shared

mitigation.strategy: Isolate the LLM client with strict timeouts, connection management, and graceful degradation
steps: The LLM client must use explicit 30-second timeout — no connection reuse across health check invocations to prevent leaked connection state
API key must be sourced from environment (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY) with a clear startup check — log a warning if missing and disable Tier 2 automatically
All LLM client errors must be caught at the HealthInspectorClient boundary — never propagate SDK exceptions to the HealthCheckRunner
Inspector failures MUST return DEGRADED/CONTINUE (as the architect specified in TD-8) — this is critical and must be enforced in code review
Add a health check for the health checker: if the LLM client fails 3+ consecutive times, disable Tier 2 for that pipeline and log an alert
Pin the anthropic SDK version in requirements to prevent unexpected breaking changes on orchestrator rebuild

risks.rollback_plan: Set an environment variable (e.g., HEALTH_TIER2_ENABLED=false) to disable the agent inspector entirely without code changes. The HealthCheckRunner should check this flag and skip Tier 2 registration.
risks.human_review_reason: This is the first time the orchestrator calls the LLM API directly. The team should confirm this is acceptable from a cost and architectural perspective. An alternative is to spawn a lightweight container for the inspector (preserving the current boundary), though this adds latency.

risks.title: Health check false positives could terminate healthy pipelines
risks.description: The architect recommends automatic FAIL_PIPELINE enforcement (TD-7): when a health check returns FAIL_PIPELINE, the runner marks the pipeline as FAILED (after consulting retry logic). A false positive — where the health check incorrectly concludes a pipeline is failing — would terminate a healthy pipeline, destroying in-progress agent work. This is particularly risky for Tier 2 (LLM-based evaluation) where the inspector might misinterpret normal agent behavior as failure. For Tier 1, the phase output presence check could false-positive if git push is slow (commits exist locally but haven't reached the remote yet when the check runs).
evidence: TD-7 specifies automatic enforcement: FAIL_PIPELINE action marks pipeline FAILED
The phase output presence check looks for commits on the remote — but git push is async and may not have completed when PHASE_COMPLETE triggers
Tier 2 uses Haiku to evaluate agent work quality — Haiku may not have sufficient context to understand all valid agent behaviors
A false positive on FAIL_PIPELINE is destructive: pipeline is terminated, containers killed, agent work potentially lost

steps: For phase output presence: check LOCAL branch head, not just remote. If local has commits but remote doesn't, return DEGRADED (not FAILED) — the push may still be in progress

No single health check should be able to trigger FAIL_PIPELINE alone. Require either: (a) FAILED from Tier 1 AND confirmed by Tier 2, or (b) FAILED from Tier 1 on a check with high confidence (e.g., all containers gone from Docker)

Add a 'confirmation delay' for FAIL_PIPELINE: on first FAILED result, store it but don't act. If the same check returns FAILED on the next trigger (e.g., next wave), then enforce. This handles transient conditions
Log every FAIL_PIPELINE action with full context (check name, reason, pipeline state snapshot) for post-mortem analysis
For Tier 2: the LLM prompt should include instructions to err on the side of DEGRADED over FAILED, and to explain its reasoning. FAILED should require clear evidence, not ambiguity

risks.rollback_plan: Change the runner to treat FAIL_PIPELINE as advisory-only (emit event but don't mutate pipeline state). This preserves observability without destructive action. Can be toggled via configuration.

risks.title: Scope and complexity of change (13 new files, 8 modified files)
risks.description: The architect's plan includes 13 implementation phases across 6 stages, creating ~13 new files in orchestrator/health/ and modifying 8 existing files (including the critical routes/pipelines.py, container_monitor.py, multi_agent.py, cli.py, api.py, models.py). This is a large change that touches the orchestrator's critical path. The migration of startup_reconciliation and container_monitor adds behavioral equivalence requirements. The testing plan calls for 5 new test files. In aggregate, this is one of the larger changes proposed for the orchestrator, estimated at 1500-2500 lines of new code.
evidence: New files: health/__init__.py, types.py, context.py, base.py, runner.py, llm_client.py, checks/__init__.py, checks/startup.py, checks/container_liveness.py, checks/phase_output.py, checks/state_consistency.py, checks/failure_patterns.py, checks/agent_inspector.py (~13 files)
Modified files: models.py, api.py, cli.py, container_monitor.py, multi_agent.py, routes/pipelines.py, routes/health.py, startup_reconciliation.py (~8 files)
Test files: test_health_types.py, test_health_context.py, test_health_checks.py, test_health_runner.py, test_health_integration.py (~5 files)

mitigation.strategy: Incremental delivery with clean merge boundaries
steps: Consider splitting into 2 PRs: PR-1 (foundation: types, interface, runner, model changes, Tier 1 checks, tests) and PR-2 (Tier 2 inspector, lifecycle wiring, integration tests)
PR-1 is independently valuable — it unifies the existing mechanisms under a common interface and adds phase output presence (which catches the issue-835 scenario)
PR-2 adds the novel capability (LLM-based semantic evaluation) and wires everything into the lifecycle
Within each PR, stage commits logically: types first, then runner, then checks, then wiring
Ensure each commit passes existing tests (no regression introduced mid-PR)

risks.rollback_plan: The orchestrator/health/ package is self-contained. To roll back: revert the wiring changes in pipelines.py, cli.py, container_monitor.py, and multi_agent.py (~20 lines of integration code). The health package can remain in the codebase without effect.

risks.title: Backward compatibility of startup reconciliation and container monitor migration
risks.description: The plan migrates two existing, battle-tested mechanisms (startup_reconciliation.py and container_monitor.py) to the new HealthCheck interface. Both currently write directly to pipeline state. The migration moves state mutation to HealthCheckRunner._apply_result(). If the migrated behavior differs in any way (different error messages, different state mutation ordering, different timing), it could break existing monitoring dashboards, log-based alerts, or orchestrator workflows that depend on the current error strings.
evidence: startup_reconciliation.py marks pipelines FAILED with specific error message 'Container not found at orchestrator startup'
container_monitor._reconcile_container_state() marks agents and pipelines FAILED with specific error messages including container IDs
Both use different locking patterns: startup reconciliation uses NO locking (runs before server starts), container monitor uses per-pipeline lock with optimistic versioning
The HealthCheckRunner._apply_result() would use a single code path for both, which may not preserve these differences

mitigation.strategy: Behavioral equivalence testing and preserved error messages
steps: Create a test that captures the EXACT current behavior of startup_reconciliation: given a pipeline with a stale container, record the resulting Pipeline object (status, error message, agent statuses). Then run the migrated StartupReconciliationCheck through the runner and assert identical output
Same for container_monitor._reconcile_container_state(): capture before/after Pipeline state and verify the migrated ContainerLivenessCheck produces identical mutations
Preserve exact error message strings in the HealthResult.reason field — the runner should copy these to pipeline.error unchanged
Keep the original functions as deprecated wrappers (as the architect recommends) for at least one release cycle

risks.rollback_plan: If migration produces behavioral differences, revert to calling the original functions directly. The HealthCheck wrappers can coexist alongside the originals — they just don't replace them yet.

risks.title: Performance impact of lazy context assembly for PipelineHealthContext
risks.description: PipelineHealthContext uses lazy-loaded properties for expensive operations (git log, git diff, agent output files). If a check inadvertently accesses a lazy property, or if the lazy implementation is not correctly cached, expensive git operations could run on every 10-second RUNTIME_TICK. The @cached_property pattern works for single-use context objects, but if the context is accidentally shared across trigger invocations, cached values become stale.
evidence: The container monitor polls every 10 seconds — RUNTIME_TICK triggers are high-frequency
git log/diff on a large repository can take 1-5 seconds depending on history depth
The ContainerLivenessCheck (RUNTIME_TICK) should ONLY access container state, never git data
If PipelineHealthContext is created once and reused across triggers (implementation bug), cached git data becomes stale

mitigation.strategy: Context is per-invocation and checks declare their data needs
steps: Create a NEW PipelineHealthContext for every run_checks() invocation — never cache or reuse across triggers

Add an assertion or type check: RUNTIME_TICK trigger should never create a context with git-related data populated. If a check running on RUNTIME_TICK accesses context.git_log, it should raise an error (fail-fast, catches interface violations early)
Document which lazy properties are 'expensive' and which checks are allowed to access them
Add a performance test: run 100 RUNTIME_TICK triggers with ContainerLivenessCheck and verify total time is under 1 second (no git operations triggered)

risks.rollback_plan: If performance degrades, add a context_mode parameter to run_checks() that creates a lightweight context for RUNTIME_TICK (no lazy git properties available) vs. a full context for PHASE_COMPLETE.

risks.title: AgentCircuitBreaker is not thread-safe and health checks run from multiple threads
risks.description: The architect's plan (TD-7) specifies that the HealthCheckRunner should consult AgentRetryManager and AgentCircuitBreaker before applying FAIL_PIPELINE actions. However, the existing AgentCircuitBreaker in shared/egg_contracts/agent_recovery.py is NOT thread-safe — it uses no locking for state transitions (CLOSED -> OPEN -> HALF_OPEN). If the runner calls circuit breaker methods from multiple threads (pipeline thread + monitor thread), the internal failure_count and state could be corrupted.
evidence: AgentCircuitBreaker.__init__() creates _failure_count, _success_count, _state without any locking primitives
record_failure() and record_success() mutate these counters without synchronization
is_open() calls _maybe_transition_to_half_open() which reads and writes _state without locks
The HealthCheckRunner will be invoked from multiple threads: pipeline execution, container monitor, HTTP request handlers

mitigation.strategy: Per-pipeline circuit breaker instances or external synchronization
steps: Create circuit breaker instances per-pipeline (not shared globally) — each pipeline gets its own instance stored in the runner's registry
Alternatively, add a threading.Lock to AgentCircuitBreaker for state transitions (small upstream change to shared/egg_contracts/agent_recovery.py)
The simpler option is per-pipeline instances since the HealthCheckRunner already has a per-pipeline mental model

If the circuit breaker is only consulted (read-only) and never mutated by health checks, the thread-safety concern is reduced — verify whether run_checks needs to call record_failure() or just is_open()

risks.rollback_plan: Skip circuit breaker consultation in the initial implementation. The runner can apply FAIL_PIPELINE directly and defer retry/circuit-breaker integration to a follow-up.

risks.title: Tier 2 LLM cost accumulation in pipelines with many review cycles
risks.description: The architect estimates ~$0.01 per pipeline for Tier 2 LLM costs. However, pipelines with multiple review cycles trigger PHASE_COMPLETE per cycle, and DEGRADED escalation at WAVE_COMPLETE adds additional calls. A pathological pipeline with many review cycles and frequent DEGRADED signals could accumulate costs.
evidence: Tier 2 runs at every PHASE_COMPLETE (TD-6)
Tier 2 also runs at WAVE_COMPLETE if Tier 1 returns DEGRADED
Review cycles can repeat multiple times per phase
Haiku costs are low (~$0.001/call) but accumulate

steps: Track Tier 2 invocation count per pipeline in the HealthCheckRunner (simple counter)
Set a per-pipeline cap on Tier 2 invocations (e.g., max 10 per pipeline) — after the cap, skip Tier 2 and log a warning
Use the existing orchestrator/metrics.py to track health check costs as a gauge
The cost is genuinely low with Haiku — this is a nice-to-have safeguard, not a blocking concern

risks.rollback_plan: Disable Tier 2 via environment variable if costs are unexpectedly high.

risks.title: Health check results capped at 10 may lose diagnostic context
risks.description: The architect specifies a rolling window of 10 health check results per PhaseExecution (TD-5). For long-running phases with many waves, earlier health check results may be evicted before they can be analyzed. If a DEGRADED signal was recorded early and later a FAILED signal occurs, the original DEGRADED context may have been evicted.
evidence: PhaseExecution.health_checks capped at 10 (TD-5)
Long implement phases can have 5+ waves, each producing 3-4 health check results
First-in-first-out eviction means early results are lost

steps: Every health check result is also emitted as an EventType.HEALTH_CHECK event — the EventBus history (100 events) provides a secondary window
For post-mortem analysis, health check events can be queried from SSE stream logs
If 10 proves insufficient, increase the cap — at ~200 bytes per result, even 50 results adds only ~10KB
Consider keeping only the most recent N results per check_name (not globally) to ensure each check type retains its latest result

risks.rollback_plan: Increase the cap or remove it entirely — the size impact is negligible.

overall_assessment.summary: The proposed architecture is sound and well-aligned with existing codebase patterns. The three high risks (pipelines.py integration, concurrency, false positives) are all manageable with the mitigations described. The medium risks (new LLM dependency, scope, backward compatibility, thread safety) require attention during implementation but are not architectural blockers. I recommend proceeding with Approach A, with two key adjustments: (1) consider splitting Tier 1 and Tier 2 into separate PRs to reduce review burden and isolate the LLM dependency introduction, and (2) implement confirmation delay for FAIL_PIPELINE actions to prevent false positive destruction of healthy pipelines.

recommendations.title: Split implementation into two PRs: Tier 1 first, Tier 2 second
recommendations.rationale: The architect recommends shipping both tiers together to validate the interface handles both cleanly. However, the risk profile differs significantly: Tier 1 is pure Python with deterministic checks and no new dependencies. Tier 2 introduces LLM API calls, a new SDK dependency, and non-deterministic evaluation. Splitting into two PRs (1) reduces review burden for the critical Tier 1 changes, (2) allows Tier 1 to be deployed and validated in production before adding Tier 2, (3) isolates the LLM dependency so it can be reverted independently if issues arise. The interface should be designed for both tiers from the start — only the implementation ships incrementally.
recommendations.trade_off: Slight risk that the interface may need adjustment when Tier 2 is added. Mitigated by designing PipelineHealthContext and HealthResult with Tier 2 fields from the start.

recommendations.title: Implement FAIL_PIPELINE confirmation delay
recommendations.rationale: Automatic pipeline termination on a health check result is powerful but dangerous. A single false positive destroys in-progress work. Implement a 'two-strike' rule: the first FAIL_PIPELINE result is recorded but not enforced. If the same check returns FAIL_PIPELINE on the next trigger (e.g., next wave complete), then enforce. This handles transient conditions (slow git push, temporary Docker API error) without weakening the detection for persistent failures.
recommendations.trade_off: Adds a small delay before pipeline termination for genuine failures (one trigger cycle). Acceptable: if a pipeline is genuinely failing, waiting one more wave cycle before terminating is not costly.

recommendations.title: Exception isolation at all integration points
recommendations.rationale: Health checks are a safety net, not a gate. An unhandled exception in a health check must NEVER crash _run_pipeline, the container monitor, or the HTTP server. Every call to HealthCheckRunner.run_checks() at an integration site must be wrapped in try/except with logging. The runner itself should catch exceptions from individual checks and return DEGRADED/CONTINUE for that check, not propagate the exception.
recommendations.trade_off: None. This is a strict requirement with no downside.

recommendations.title: Add a kill-switch for health check enforcement
recommendations.rationale: Provide an environment variable (e.g., HEALTH_CHECK_MODE=enforce|observe|disabled) to control behavior without code changes. 'enforce' applies FAIL_PIPELINE actions. 'observe' emits events but never mutates pipeline state. 'disabled' skips all health checks. Start with 'observe' in production, switch to 'enforce' once confidence is established.
recommendations.trade_off: Adds a small amount of configuration complexity. Worth it for operational safety during rollout.

recommendations.title: Behavioral equivalence tests for migrated mechanisms
recommendations.rationale: The startup reconciliation and container monitor migrations must produce EXACTLY the same observable behavior (error messages, pipeline state, agent state). Create snapshot-style tests: run the original function and the migrated HealthCheck on the same input, assert the resulting Pipeline objects are identical. This catches subtle differences that code review might miss.
recommendations.trade_off: Adds test maintenance burden. Worth it for the confidence it provides during migration.

recommendations.title: Consider spawning Tier 2 inspector as a lightweight container instead of in-process LLM calls
recommendations.rationale: The current architecture has a clean boundary: the orchestrator manages pipelines, containers make LLM calls. Introducing LLM calls into the orchestrator blurs this boundary. An alternative is to spawn a short-lived container for the inspector agent, which preserves the existing boundary and reuses the container spawning infrastructure. The downside is additional latency (container startup) and complexity. The in-process approach is simpler and faster — but the team should explicitly decide whether they want to maintain the boundary.
recommendations.trade_off: Container-based inspector adds 10-30 seconds of latency per check (container startup) vs. 1-2 seconds for in-process. In-process is preferred for speed but breaks an architectural boundary.

areas_needing_human_review.reason: The decision between automatic enforcement (TD-7) vs. advisory-only significantly affects pipeline reliability. Automatic enforcement with false positives destroys in-progress work. Advisory-only risks being ignored. The confirmation delay (REC-2) and observe mode (REC-4) are compromise positions. The team should decide the initial enforcement policy.

areas_needing_human_review.area: Tier 2 delivery timing (same PR vs. follow-up)
areas_needing_human_review.reason: The architect recommends shipping both tiers together. The risk assessment recommends splitting (REC-1). Both have valid rationale. The team should decide based on their risk tolerance and review capacity.

areas_needing_human_review.area: In-process LLM calls vs. container-based inspector
areas_needing_human_review.reason: The orchestrator currently makes zero LLM API calls. Introducing this dependency is a meaningful architectural decision that should be deliberate, not implicit. The team should confirm this is acceptable.

The exact lines in _run_pipeline() where health checks are wired in need review by someone familiar with the control flow. The 5543-line file has many edge cases (short-circuit paths, error recovery, review cycles) that the health check integration must not disrupt.

details: No new external attack surface: the on-demand health check endpoint (POST /api/v1/pipelines/{id}/health-check) follows the same authentication/authorization pattern as existing pipeline endpoints
No secrets in health check results: HealthResult contains check_name, status, reason, and action — no credentials, tokens, or sensitive data
Tier 2 LLM calls use ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from environment (not hardcoded). The API key is already available via the gateway proxy in both network modes
Health check results persisted in pipeline state JSON use the same access controls as existing pipeline data
PipelineHealthContext does not expose raw Docker API access to checks — checks receive structured data, not the Docker client object
New HealthCheckResult field in PhaseExecution uses default_factory=list — existing pipelines without health_checks will deserialize correctly with an empty list
Startup reconciliation and container monitor keep their original functions as deprecated wrappers — no API breakage for external callers
EventType.HEALTH_CHECK already exists in the EventType enum — no event type migration needed
New health check REST endpoint is additive — no changes to existing endpoint signatures
The health/ package is new — no namespace collisions with existing code

unit_tests: Each HealthCheck implementation with mock PipelineHealthContext: verify correct HealthResult for healthy, degraded, and failed scenarios
HealthCheckRunner: trigger filtering, Tier 1->Tier 2 escalation, result capping, exception handling for individual check failures
PipelineHealthContext: lazy loading verified (expensive properties not computed until accessed), per-invocation isolation
LLM client: timeout handling, malformed response handling, API error handling, graceful degradation to DEGRADED/CONTINUE
integration_tests: Behavioral equivalence: migrated startup reconciliation produces identical Pipeline state as original
Behavioral equivalence: migrated container monitor produces identical Pipeline state as original
Lifecycle wiring: STARTUP trigger runs startup checks, RUNTIME_TICK runs container liveness, WAVE_COMPLETE runs Tier 1, PHASE_COMPLETE runs both tiers
Exception isolation: health check exception does not crash _run_pipeline, container monitor, or HTTP handler
concurrency_tests: Multiple threads invoking run_checks() on the same pipeline simultaneously — verify no VersionConflictError goes unhandled
Health check running while _run_pipeline saves phase transition — verify no deadlock or lost update
Container monitor handler and on_wave_complete callback firing simultaneously — verify correct pipeline state
performance_tests: 100 RUNTIME_TICK triggers with ContainerLivenessCheck — total time under 1 second, no git operations triggered
PHASE_COMPLETE with Tier 2 inspector — total time under 35 seconds (30s LLM timeout + 5s overhead)
Pipeline state size with 10 HealthCheckResults — verify under 3KB additional per phase

agreement: Approach A (unified HealthCheck interface) is the correct choice — the abstraction pays for itself immediately
The HealthCheck/HealthResult/PipelineHealthContext trio provides a testable, composable model that replaces ad-hoc mechanisms
Lazy context assembly (TD-2) is the right approach for avoiding unnecessary git operations on high-frequency triggers
Haiku for Tier 2 (TD-3) is appropriate for structured evaluation tasks — cost-effective and fast
Pure checks with centralized result application (TD-4) is the right separation of concerns
PhaseExecution.health_checks is the natural home for results (TD-5)
EventType.HEALTH_CHECK already exists — infrastructure is ready
The implementation staging (types -> runner -> migration -> new checks -> wiring -> tests) is well-ordered
concerns: The architect recommends shipping Tier 1 and Tier 2 together (recommended_approach justification point 3). This increases risk and review burden. The interface can be designed for both tiers while shipping Tier 1 first.
TD-7 (automatic FAIL_PIPELINE) lacks a false-positive protection mechanism. The 'confirmation delay' pattern should be explicitly incorporated into the runner design.

The architect's RISK-1 (integration complexity for pipelines.py) correctly rates it as 'high impact, medium likelihood' but the mitigation ('single runner.run_checks() calls') understates the risk of exception propagation from health checks into the pipeline execution thread.
The architect does not address that execute_all_waves() at line 3260 is currently called WITHOUT an on_wave_complete callback — this is a calling pattern change that deserves explicit attention.
Missing risk: the orchestrator has zero existing Anthropic SDK usage. This dependency introduction deserves its own risk entry (captured as RISK-3 in this assessment).
additional_risks_identified: RISK-3 (new LLM dependency in orchestrator) — not in architect's risk list
RISK-4 (false positive pipeline termination) — architect mentions LLM reliability (risk-4) but not the broader false positive concern for both tiers
RISK-8 (AgentCircuitBreaker thread safety) — not in architect's analysis
